Article Title: Separated from their own, these Kuno cheetahs found brothers in each other
Article Text:
An unlikely bond: Male cheetahs CCB4 (left) and KNG23 (right) have come to enjoy each other’s company





BHOPAL: One was born in India while the other flew thousands of kilometres by a special aircraft from Botswana. Though born to different mothers, they are brothers, not by blood but bonding. Deep in the wilds of Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno, two male cheetahs — coded as KNG23 and CCB4 — have developed an unusual social bond, offering a rare insight into how these felines can form lifelong relationships despite not growing up together.Their story, highlighted in the latest newsletter issued by Kuno authorities, has emerged as one of the most unusual behavioural developments in four remarkable years of Project Cheetah.KNG23 was born in India to cheetah Nirva, while CCB4 was among the felines translocated from the African wilds of Botswana. The two unrelated males were brought together after separate periods of isolation. What began as a cautious introduction has evolved into a close social association, with the two now following each other, hunting and feeding together, calling to each other and even grooming one another.The Kuno field team has also observed the two supporting each other when challenged by another coalition.Such behaviour has prompted the team to closely monitor whether their association develops into a stable coalition.Male cheetahs are typically social animals, known to form coalitions, most commonly between brothers from the same litter. Such groups can help males defend territories, hunt and protect kills, patrol their range and confront rivals and predators.KNG23 and CCB4, however, do not fit the familiar pattern. They are unrelated, coming from different countries and growing up in different habitats.However, the stories of how they got separated from their own do bear an uncanny similarity. KNG23 was separated from his mother, brother and sister around March 2026, after suffering a minor injury that required isolation, while CCB4 was separated from his two sisters around the same period.The two males were subsequently introduced to each other.Even after KNG23 recovered and was reunited with his family, he continued to show an interest in CCB4 while the two remained separated by a fence. KNG23 was released into the wild with his mother, brother and sister on May 30. After several weeks, he was injured again in late July and brought back for treatment. By then, CCB4 was alone, as his two sisters had moved into the wild. The two males were again placed close to each other to explore whether their association could develop further.Their first introduction was peaceful. When the fence was removed, both appeared relaxed and comfortable in each other’s presence. The crucial test came when a kill was provided. However, even the prey could put a strain on their relationship, as they both shared the meal without showing any aggression or confrontation.Over the following days, stronger signs of social bonding emerged. KNG23 began following CCB4 closely and sitting beside him. They continued hunting and feeding together. When one moved out of sight, the other responded with the characteristic chirping call used by cheetahs to maintain contact. They were also observed grooming each other, Kuno officials noted in the newsletter.The field team said the two are now displaying several behaviours associated with coalition formation, including remaining together, following one another, hunting and feeding together and mutual grooming.Officials, however, cautioned that sharing a kill or spending time together alone does not establish a coalition. If the association develops into a stable coalition, it could potentially be the first documented coalition between two unrelated male cheetahs originating from different countries, they added.
Article Summary: KNG23 was born in India to cheetah Nirva, while CCB4 was among the felines translocated from the African wilds of Botswana. The two unrelated males were brought together after separate periods of isolation. What began as a cautious introduction has evolved into a close social association.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu on AI doom fears: ‘Without scientific scepticism, we risk being delusional’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

Sridhar Vembu says AI scepticism must stay grounded in science

James Maynard says he was wrong about AI predictions

Sridhar Vembu says conviction and scepticism both matter

Zoho founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu has shared his view on the growing debate over whether AI could pose serious risks to humanity. Sridhar Vembu said he has not bought into AI doom scenarios, but believes people should remain open to changing their views as AI models become more capable. Vembu was responding to a post by American physicist Steve Hsu, who shared comments from Fields Medalist James Maynard on X. Maynard said he had been sceptical of earlier AI predictions that sounded like science fiction but now takes the risks more seriously because many of those predictions have proved more accurate than he expected.Sridhar Vembu said people need both personal conviction and scientific scepticism when thinking about AI and its future.“I have not bought into the AI doom scenarios,” Vembu wrote on X, pointing to Maynard's changing position as an example of what he described as a scientific attitude.“Fields Medalist James Maynard teaches us the scientific attitude about this: he has been highly sceptical of claims of AI doom but as the models demonstrate higher and higher capability levels, he is taking them more seriously now.”Steve Hsu's post quoted Maynard discussing how his view of AI risks has changed.Maynard said he had followed AI for some time but had been sceptical of predictions that appeared to come from science fiction.“I've been interested and I've been following AI, but I've heard all these predictions that just sound like sci-fi and I've been consistently dismissive and skeptical of all of them.”He then acknowledged that his earlier view had been wrong.“But I've been consistently wrong. The people who sound like they're talking from a sci-fi novel are the people who've been making much much more accurate predictions.”Maynard concluded that AI risks should not simply be dismissed as hype.Vembu said personal conviction helps people continue working toward a goal, while scientific scepticism can prevent people from becoming disconnected from evidence.“Our own hunches and convictions allow us to pursue and stick to a course of action and scientific scepticism keeps us grounded in reality,” he wrote.He added:“Without a strong internal conviction, our actions lack the will power to succeed. Without scientific scepticism, we risk being delusional.”
Article Summary: Sridhar Vembu says people need both personal conviction and scientific scepticism when thinking about AI and its future. He was responding to a post by American physicist Steve Hsu, who shared comments from Fields Medalist James Maynard. Maynard said he had been sceptical of earlier AI predictions that sounded like science fiction but now takes the risks more seriously.

Article Title: Offshore wind farms may be quietly stealing rain from Europe's coasts; study says: The more energy turbines pull from the wind, the less...
Article Text:
Representative image

Turbines slow the wind and stir up the air above the sea

Ten years of weather data went into the North Sea rainfall model

The study tested an extreme wind buildout, not Europe's actual plan

Europe is counting on offshore wind to move away from fossil fuels, and the North Sea is at the centre of that plan. The European Union wants 300 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2050. A new study from Germany suggests turbines at that scale could do more than generate electricity. They could also change where rain falls.Researchers at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon found that very large offshore wind farm clusters may push more rain over the sea and leave parts of the coastline drier. In their simulations, coastal areas in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom saw rainfall drop by up to 15%. The findings were published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.A wind turbine works by taking energy out of moving air. The wind behind it ends up slower and more turbulent.That turbulence mixes different layers of the atmosphere. Moist air gets pushed upward, where it cools, condenses and forms clouds. The result is more rain directly over the wind farms.The catch is that air can only carry so much moisture. When more of it falls over the sea, less is left by the time the air reaches land.Coastal regions downwind get less rain as a result.The team at Hereon's Institute of Coastal Systems - Analysis and Modeling used a high-resolution regional climate model called COSMO-CLM. The simulations ran on weather data from 2008 to 2017. Using a full decade smoothed out the effect of any single unusual year and gave a clearer view of long-term patterns.The model included existing wind farms and every zone marked for future development across the North Sea and the Baltic Sea."Our work helps ensure that the further expansion of offshore wind energy in Europe can be aligned with the requirements of climate protection, environmental protection and coastal management," said Dr Naveed Akhtar, the study's lead author.The scenario was extreme by design. The researchers assumed maximum turbine deployment across all designated areas, which pushed installed capacity well past the 300 GW target. The goal was to make any climate effect large enough to detect and measure. It is not a forecast of what Europe will build.The results also describe long-term weather averages. They do not mean a specific town will miss rain on a specific day. Earlier Hereon research has shown that farm size, layout and turbine spacing affect how strongly turbines change the atmosphere, so a smaller or more spread-out buildout may have a milder effect.So will Europe's coasts lose rain? That depends on how the continent builds. The researchers are not arguing against offshore wind. They want more realistic scenarios tested for turbine density, farm size and placement, and they plan to study effects on the ocean and marine life next. For countries that share the same weather systems, where a wind farm goes may matter as much as how much power it produces.
Article Summary: Turbines slow the wind and stir up the air above the sea. Moist air gets pushed upward, where it cools, condenses and forms clouds. The result is more rain directly over the wind farms. When more of it falls over the sea, less is left by the time the air reaches land.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
Article Text:
A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. It quietly brings attention to something that a lot of people who use the internet notice but don't often say out loud. People in different communities often have a bigger impact on each other than they think.The conversation begins with a confident and lighthearted comment from one of the trans women present. She says, "You know that trans women are like the OG lip masters, right? We are very talented in the program. Like, I do the peptides, I'm on Zeta." Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle.He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." It’s not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.

Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration.

Article Title: Woman shot dead by husband after quarrel over cooking vegetables in Delhi, say police

A Delhi woman was allegedly shot dead by her husband following a domestic quarrel.





NEW DELHI: A 31-year-old woman was allegedly shot dead by her husband following a quarrel over cooking vegetables at their home in Delhi’s Tigri area on Friday evening, police said.The accused, identified as Kamlesh, allegedly tried to mislead neighbours by claiming that his wife, Poonam, had shot herself. However, residents grew suspicious, caught him as he tried to leave and handed him over to police, officials said.The incident took place around 7pm at the couple’s house in Tigri, Sangam Vihar. According to police, the couple had an argument over the preparation of vegetables, which escalated before Kamlesh allegedly shot Poonam.Poonam died at the spot, police said.Residents said they heard a loud sound from inside the house and knocked on the door. Kamlesh allegedly did not open it for some time. The couple’s three children, who were inside the house, were heard crying, prompting neighbours to repeatedly ask him to open the door.Kamlesh allegedly then tried to leave the house, telling neighbours that Poonam had shot herself. Suspicious of his account, residents caught him and alerted police.A police team reached the spot and took Kamlesh into custody. Poonam’s body was sent for post-mortem examination. Further investigation is underway, police said.
Article Summary: A 31-year-old woman was allegedly shot dead by her husband following a quarrel over cooking vegetables. The accused, identified as Kamlesh, allegedly tried to mislead neighbours by claiming that his wife, Poonam, had shot herself. However, residents grew suspicious, caught him as he tried to leave and handed him over to police.

Article Title: ‘Want some peace for important deal’: Ex-employee, partner sent texts to family from executive’s phone after Gurgaon murder
Article Text:
According to Delhi Police, Yuvraj was murdered by Anya Vats (L) and Sanyam Sachdeva.

.

kada

Suspects sent his family texts





NEW DELHI: “Our mother is waiting for me to bring back something – anything to remember Yuvraj by. His clothes, his watch… or now, even his ashes,” said Karishma Manchanda, the older sister of Yuvraj Singh Manchanda (31), a project manager at Adani Realty, who was killed allegedly by two of his former colleagues, his body dumped in a drain in Gurgaon.While his body was found by Haryana Police on Sept 10, the family didn’t find out till Sept 16His body had been cremated by cops in the interim. Karishma said her family has still not been given his remains. She told TOIit was only when she went to the Badshahpur police station in Gurgaon on Sept 16 that she realised her brother’s body had been found six days ago and had already been cremated.According to Delhi Police, Yuvraj was murdered by Anya Vats and Sanyam Sachdeva, his former colleagues at a real estate firm, on Sept 6.His family eventually learnt that he had died after Delhi Police apprehended Vats and Sachdeva from Uttarakhand, following which they confessed to their crime.The family alleged that Haryana Police did not follow protocol and didn’t upload Yuvraj’s photo on Zipnet — a portal used by police in different states to share information about missing or unknown dead persons.After they filed the missing complaint, the family and friends checked Zipnet every day for any information.Details of missing or unknown deceased persons are uploaded on Zipnet or CCTNS for family members to identify them. “Every hour of the day, we would check Zipnet. There was no update,” said Rajat Jain.Karishma and one of Yuvraj’s friends, Sahil, went to Badshahpur police station on Sept 16. “We saw Yuvraj’s picture. Police said he was found in a drain on Sept 10. We were shocked to hear that his body had been cremated by police on Sept 14,” Sahil said.Haryana Police, as per the info­r­mation on Zipnet, uploaded his de­tails only on Sept 16. They, however, said Zipnet was not the principal pan-India system being used for unidentified bodies and maintained the details were uploaded on CCTNS as part of the prescribed process on Sept 11. “Had the information been uploaded on Zipnet as soon as they found his body, at least we would have been able to perform his last rites and grieve,” Jain said.Karishma, meanwhile, also said she was made to wait for five hours when she went to Badshahpur poli­ce station for information about her dead brother’s belongings. After two days, the family is yet to receive anything — his ashes, clothes, a, his gold ring or even the postmortem report. Sahil said police told them that they had “given away” his clothes, as they were “stinking”.For two days after they saw him last on Sept 6, Karishma and her parents received messages from Yuvraj Singh Manchanda’s phone telling them he was working on an “important deal” and wanted “peace”. He refused to take their calls. A message on Sept 7 said he was flying to Bengaluru for work that day, along with a photo of a ticket. The last message came a day later, asking them not to disturb him and saying that he would call two days later.Only, Yuvraj had been killed on Sept 6. The promised call never came and Yuvraj’s family hit the panic button on Sept 11, filing a missing person complaint at Delhi’s Lajpat Nagar police station.According to Delhi Police, it was Vats and Sachdeva who kept sending messages to Yuvraj’s family members and friends to keep the ruse alive and prevent them from approaching the police.Karishma recalled that when she received his messages after Sept 6, she begged him to call, show his face or even send a voice note. “My younger sister got a message saying he would call her on Sept 10. When his phone was switched off on that day, we panicked and filed a missing persons complaint,” she said.A project manager at Adani Realty, Yuvraj was described by his friends as a passionate and dedicated employee. Hours before he disappeared, he had bought a sherwani from Lajpat Nagar for his wedding, which was scheduled for Oct.“Our mother is a heart patient and our father is paralysed. Yuvraj would come back by 10pm every day to take care of them. Now, we can only hope of getting his ashes home,” Karishma said.
Article Summary: Yuvraj Singh Manchanda, a project manager at Adani Realty, was killed allegedly by two of his former colleagues, his body dumped in a drain in Gurgaon. According to Delhi Police, Yuvraj was murdered by Anya Vats and Sanyam Sachdeva. While his body was found by Haryana Police on Sept 10, the family didn’t find out till Sept 16.

Article Title: Man arrested for murder of friend in Pandara Park jhuggi
Article Text: New Delhi: A man was apprehended for killing his friend over an old dispute by hitting him in the head with a blunt object. The body was found after residents complained of a foul smell coming from a jhuggi at Pandara Park.Following this, two teams were set up by Tilak Marg police station tasked with examination of footage from more than 100 CCTV cameras installed near the place of occurrence and along adjoining routes. It was found that the suspect, Rakesh , had escaped using the deceased’s motorcycle. He had fled to Chatrapati Sambhaji Nagar in Maharashtra, from where he was apprehended following a raid.
